parts.title: Moving house
parts.context: A woman phones a removals company for a quote.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a removals company to ask for a quote. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: tony
script.text: Morning, Swift Removals, Tony speaking.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Hello. I'm moving house next month and I'd like a quote, please. At the moment I live in a flat.

script.speaker: tony
script.text: Right, a flat. Let me take some details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The woman lives in a flat, so 'flat' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: tony
script.text: Can I have your name, please?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Anna Whitfield. That's W-H-I-T-F-I-E-L-D.

script.speaker: tony
script.text: Thanks, Anna. And where are you moving to?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: My company wanted me to transfer to the York office, but in the end they agreed to Leeds, which is where my family is. So it's Leeds.

script.speaker: tony
script.text: Leeds. And how big is the new place?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: The flat I'm in now has two bedrooms, and the new house has three. So I'll have a lot more space.

script.speaker: tony
script.text: Lucky you. Are there any very large or heavy items we should know about?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Well, there's a sofa. I did have a piano, but I've sold it. The real problem is an old oak bookcase that my grandfather made. It's enormous and very heavy, and I don't want it damaged.

script.speaker: tony
script.text: We'll wrap it properly, don't worry. Is there anything about the new house that could make it difficult for us? Steps, parking, that kind of thing?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: There's plenty of parking, but the lane leading up to the house is very narrow. I'm not sure a large lorry would get through.

script.speaker: tony
script.text: In that case we'll send two smaller vans instead. Thanks for telling me.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: tony
script.text: Would you like us to do the packing for you?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: I'll pack my books and clothes myself. But could you pack the kitchen? There are a lot of glasses and plates, and I always break something.

script.speaker: tony
script.text: Of course, that's very common. Do you need any storage? Sometimes people can't move in straight away.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Actually, yes. The new house won't be ready for a while, so I'll need storage for about two weeks. No, wait, the builders said three weeks to be safe. Let's say three.

script.speaker: tony
script.text: Three weeks. Fine. Now, before we can give you an exact price, someone has to come and look at your flat. Could we do that on Wednesday?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: I'm working all day Wednesday. Thursday would be better.

script.speaker: tony
script.text: Thursday's fine. Morning or afternoon?

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Mornings are difficult, because I start early. Could it be in the afternoon, after two?

script.speaker: tony
script.text: No problem, I'll put you down for Thursday afternoon. And then we'll send you the quote. Most people like it by email.

script.speaker: anna
script.text: Normally I would, but my laptop's broken at the moment, so could you send it by post?

script.speaker: tony
script.text: Of course. It'll be with you by the end of next week.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A science museum
parts.context: A guide welcomes a group of visitors to a science museum.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a guide welcoming a group of visitors to a science museum. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Hi, everyone, and welcome to the Discovery Science Museum. My name's Helen, and I'm going to give you a quick introduction before you explore on your own.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: The museum opened in nineteen sixty-two in an old railway station, which is why the main hall has that wonderful glass roof. It was rebuilt ten years ago, and since then the number of visitors has more than doubled, mainly because almost everything is now hands-on. Our aim is that you learn by doing, not just by reading labels.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Entry to the main galleries is free, as you know. The only things you pay for are the planetarium shows, which cost four dollars. You can buy tickets at the information desk, but they often sell out by lunchtime, so I'd buy them now rather than later.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: If you've brought your own food, you're welcome to eat it in the picnic room on the ground floor. Please don't eat in the galleries, though. The café on the top floor has great views, but it's quite small, and it gets very busy between twelve and two.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: We also lend out a few things that you might find useful. Strollers can be borrowed free of charge from the cloakroom, and so can wheelchairs. We used to lend audio guides too, but they've been replaced by a free app, which you can download using the museum's wi-fi.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: And one last thing: the museum closes at five, but the galleries start to close at a quarter to, so please make your way to the exit in good time.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Now, let me tell you a little about our three main galleries. On the first floor is the Space gallery. Everyone's favourite there is the moon-landing simulator, but it's popular, so expect a queue. The Space gallery is also where you'll find our new temporary exhibition, on the search for water on Mars. It's only here until the end of the month.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: The Human Body gallery is on the second floor. It has a giant model of a heart that you can walk through, and lots of objects you're actually allowed to handle, including real bones and a human brain preserved in plastic. Don't worry, it's quite safe to touch.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: The Energy gallery is next to it, on the same floor. There's a live science show there every hour, on the hour, where our staff do experiments with electricity. They're very noisy and very popular.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: If you have small children, the Energy gallery also has a special section for under-fives, with water play and building blocks. It's the only gallery that has one, so it gets busy.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: And finally, the Human Body gallery has just installed a new interactive game, where you race against the clock to deliver oxygen around the body. We'd love to know what you think of it, so there's a short feedback form beside it. Enjoy your visit.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A dissertation on language apps
parts.context: A student discusses her dissertation on language-learning apps with her tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear a student, Kim, discussing her dissertation on language-learning apps with her tutor, Dr Reed. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: reed
script.text: Hi Kim, come in. How's the dissertation going?

script.speaker: kim
script.text: Better than last time, I think. I've narrowed down my research question, like you suggested. I'm now looking only at adult beginners learning Spanish with apps.

script.speaker: reed
script.text: Good. Why adult beginners in particular?

script.speaker: kim
script.text: Partly because there's less research on adults than on schoolchildren. But mainly because when I looked at the app companies' own data, adult beginners were the group most likely to give up in the first month. I wanted to know why.

script.speaker: reed
script.text: That's a strong reason. And how are you collecting your data?

script.speaker: kim
script.text: I'd planned to do a big online survey, but I realised it wouldn't tell me why people give up. So instead I'm following twelve learners for eight weeks. They keep a short learning diary, and I interview them every fortnight.

script.speaker: reed
script.text: Twelve is a small sample, but for this kind of study it's fine, as long as you explain that in your methodology. Now, I read your literature review. It's well organised, but it's mostly a list of what each study found. I'd like to see you comparing the studies and pointing out where they disagree.

script.speaker: kim
script.text: OK, I'll work on that. I've had one practical problem too. Two of my learners have already dropped out of the study.

script.speaker: reed
script.text: That happens. In fact, it's data in itself. Could you ask them why they stopped?

script.speaker: kim
script.text: I hadn't thought of that. One of them said it was because of work, but I could ask them both for a short interview.

script.speaker: reed
script.text: Do that. It might turn out to be the most interesting part of the whole project.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: reed
script.text: What have your learners said so far about the different features of the apps?

script.speaker: kim
script.text: Quite a lot. The daily streak, where the app counts how many days in a row you've practised, came up in nearly every diary. People say it really keeps them going. One woman said she practised on her wedding day just so she didn't lose her streak.

script.speaker: reed
script.text: And the speech recognition?

script.speaker: kim
script.text: That was the biggest complaint. Several learners said the app accepted their pronunciation when it was obviously wrong, and then rejected it when it was fine. So they stopped trusting it.

script.speaker: reed
script.text: What about the leaderboards, where you compete with other learners?

script.speaker: kim
script.text: Interestingly, most of my learners said they made them feel nervous, especially when they dropped down the table. A couple of people switched them off completely.

script.speaker: reed
script.text: And the new chat feature, where you talk to an artificial partner?

script.speaker: kim
script.text: Hardly anyone has used it. It's hidden in a menu, and most people didn't even know it existed.

script.speaker: reed
script.text: And finally, the flashcards.

script.speaker: kim
script.text: Everyone agreed that the flashcard reviews were the best way to remember new words. Several said they'd learned more vocabulary that way than in any course they'd done before.

script.speaker: reed
script.text: Very interesting. Write all that up, and send me a draft of the findings chapter next month.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: desert locusts
parts.context: A lecture on desert locusts, how swarms form and how they are controlled.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about desert locusts. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Today I'm going to talk about one of the most destructive pests in the world: the desert locust. For most of the time, desert locusts are harmless. They live alone, scattered across the deserts of North Africa, the Middle East and South Asia, and they avoid each other.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Everything changes after heavy rain. Rain makes plants grow in the desert, the locusts breed rapidly, and then, as the plants dry up, large numbers of them are forced together on the few green areas that remain. That's when something remarkable happens.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Experiments have shown that the trigger is touch. When a locust is repeatedly bumped on its back legs by other locusts, its body produces more of a chemical called serotonin. Within a few hours, its behaviour changes completely. Instead of avoiding other locusts, it starts to seek them out, and over a few generations even its colour changes, from green to yellow and black.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Once they gather, they form swarms that can contain billions of insects. A swarm can travel 150 kilometres in a single day, carried by the wind. And each locust eats roughly its own weight in fresh food every day, so a swarm can strip a farmer's fields in a few hours.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: How do countries fight back? For decades, the main method has been spraying pesticides, from planes and from vehicles. This works, but the chemicals don't only kill locusts. They also harm bees and other insects, as well as birds that eat the poisoned locusts.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So scientists have developed alternatives. The most promising is a natural fungus that kills only locusts and grasshoppers and is harmless to other wildlife. Its weakness is that it is slow: it takes about a week to work, so it's best used early, before swarms form.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: That's why early warning is so important. Satellites now detect patches of green vegetation in the desert after rain, which show where locusts are likely to breed. And on the ground, farmers and survey teams report sightings using a phone app, which sends the location straight to national control centres.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Finally, some people are looking at locusts as a resource rather than just a problem. Locusts are rich in protein, and in some countries they're collected and dried to be used as animal feed, or even eaten by people. Of course, this can only ever be part of the solution, but it shows how our view of a pest can change.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
